This is an idea that was in vogue about ten years ago (maybe more now, I'm getting older every day and it's getting harder to keep up with how much time has passed). It was called peak oil, and the basic idea is that we were eventually going to run out of oil. What actually happened is we ran out of easily accessible oil.

There is a basic Geology lesson at the heart of this, so I'm going to go over that first.

A rock is an aggregate of one or more minerals. The minerals are crystals that are held together in a matrix of finer mineral crystals, cements, or even just pressure in a few cases. Rocks are classified into three groups: Igneous - which is lava that solidified on earths surface, or magma that never made it to the surface and solidified underground, Metamorphic - which was (usually) buried where it was subjected to intense heat and/or pressure that was strong enough to alter the crystal lattice and in some cases chemical composition of the minerals, and sedimentary which is where a rock breaks down into it gravel, sand, and clay/silt and is carried to a lower area where it deposits, is buried, and over time turns back into rock.

Oil has to do with sedimentary rock. Of sedimentary rocks there are different types, the two most important for our purposes are sandstone and shale. Sandstone is composed of grains of sand held together in a matrix. Sand in this instance refers to the size of the grains rather than the chemical composition. You can for instance have sandstone that is made of lime sand, or olivine. It doesn't necessarily have to be quartz, though quartz is hard and stable, so it's very common in sandstone. Sandstones usually are composed of rounded grains suspended in a matrix. The matrix can be silt and clay, or cement, or whatever. It's just the bits of rock that are smaller than the sand that glue the rock together. Commonly though there is liquid in the matrix. When it's liquid water this is called an aquifer, and people drill into it to get water out. Since the sand grains are rounded there is a lot of room for the water to flow around the sand grains.

Organic material is deposited along with the sand and over time the sand lithifies (turns to stone), while the organic matter breaks down w/out access to oxygen, meaning that the hydrocarbon chains cannot be digested by bacteria. This creates sandstone with crude oil in the matrix. Since the sand grains are rounded you can drill into this rock and start pumping oil out, and more oil will flow into the drill hole until there is no more oil in the rock. What happened towards the end of the last century is that most of these oil wells have been pumped dry.

Shales are a type of sedimentary rock that are made of clay and silt which are smaller grains than sand. These smaller grains get flattened out when they are buried and they create what is called an aquiclude. Basically, where they have flattened grains that lock together liquid doesn't flow through them. When organic matter gets buried in mud, the hydrocarbons are stuck inside the matrix of the shale, where they don't flow freely. This is called oil shale. What we do to get liquid out of them is we'll drill horizontally through a layer of shale and then we'll pump a liquid down into them that explodes under pressure (like diesel fuel) which fractures the rock, allowing the oil to flow freely. This is called hydraulic fracturing, or fracking. Fracking is a new technology that only became economically viable after most of the easier wells have been pumped dry.

Basically we developed a technology to get oil to flow freely from rock where it wouldn't before as soon as we ran out of easily accessible oil. Since oil is made up of dead critters there has been about 500 million years worth of dead animals to turn into oil, and about 2.5 billion years worth of bacteria that turns into oil when it dies and is buried in an anaerobic environment. 2.5 billion years worth of dead stuff will provide us will lots and lots of oil, though a lot of it will not be easily accessible. We're going to go through the easiest stuff first since it cost less to do so, and as the prices go up, the harder stuff to get to will become more economically viable.

What this means is that the short answer to your question is no, we're not going to run out of oil any time soon (even in the next 50 years), but it's going to get more expensive as time goes on to get it out of the ground. What's more, the deeper something is buried, the harder it is for us to see. Normally what happens is we'll wait for an earthquake to provide us with sound waves that we use to take what amounts to an ultrasound of the earth. We'll also use explosions to create these sound waves as well. The problem is that we need larger sounds to see further down, but louder sounds have larger sound waves, meaning our resolution goes down (because you can't see anything smaller than the sound waves) the further we look down.

As time goes on we're going to have to drill deeper and into rock that it's harder to get oil out of, meaning that the oil we get out is going to be more expensive. Given our current technology, it's going to be harder to detect smaller pockets of oil deeper down, but as our technology gets better we're going to keep finding more.

Love is developed in two ways. Let's use the analogy of fire. The time that's burning is love:

Attraction is the hot flame of a candle. It's easy to start, burns for a while, but ultimately it will run out.
